content: Fructose 6-phosphate, also referred to as the Neuberg ester, is a fructose sugar molecule that is phosphorylated at the sixth carbon position, classifying it as a fructose phosphate. The β-D form of fructose 6-phosphate is the predominant form found in cells. A significant proportion of glucose and fructose entering a cell is eventually converted into this compound during metabolic processes. The term Neuberg ester is derived from Carl Neuberg, a German biochemist who contributed to its discovery. In 1918, Carl Neuberg discovered that this compound, which was later identified as fructose 6-phosphate, could be synthesized through mild acid hydrolysis of the Harden-Young ester, now known as fructose 2,6-bisphosphate. Fructose 6-phosphate plays a critical role in the glycolytic pathway. It is formed through the isomerization of glucose 6-phosphate and subsequently undergoes further phosphorylation to produce fructose-1,6-bisphosphate, a key intermediate in glycolysis. Fructose 6-phosphate exists biologically in only one active isomeric form, the β-D form. While other isomers of fructose 6-phosphate exist, they are analogous to the isomers of fructose and are not biologically active.
